interpretation: Target-aware adaptive planning never required more worst-case diagnostic actions than full-world identification and strictly saved actions in 76/272 eligible rows.

The target-aware and world-aware planners chose different first actions in 24 rows, and in 23 of those the target-aware first action gave a strictly better worst-case split of reachability target classes.
Source identity was the most frequent target-optimal first action, but barrier and analyst-rule measurements were also optimal, so the planner is not a fixed measurement order.

The target-aware planner stopped with multiple worlds in 90 rows and with multiple worlds plus multiple sources in 18 rows, demonstrating that ecological target identification can legitimately leave history unresolved.
claim_boundary: The three diagnostic actions are known-truth categorical measurements with unit cost, not field-cost-equivalent observations.
Worst-case adaptive depth is a finite decision-tree quantity, not expected information gain.
Target identification does not imply historical-world or source identity.
